content: Mustard oil refers to two distinct types of oil derived from mustard seeds. The first type is a fatty vegetable oil obtained by pressing the seeds, while the second type is an essential oil produced by grinding the seeds, mixing them with water, and extracting the volatile oil through distillation. Mustard Oil from Pressed Seeds This type of mustard oil is characterized by a strong aroma, reminiscent of pungent cabbage, and a hot, nutty flavor. It is widely used for cooking in regions such as Orissa, Bengal, Bihar, and other parts of India and Bangladesh. In northern India, it is particularly popular for frying fritters. Approximately 30% of mustard seeds are composed of this oil, which can be extracted from black mustard (Brassica nigra), brown Indian mustard (Brassica juncea), and white mustard (Brassica hirta). The oil primarily consists of fatty acids such as oleic acid, linoleic acid, and erucic acid. Notably, mustard seed oil has the lowest saturated fat content among edible oils, at just 5%. In India, it is customary to heat the oil almost to its smoking point before using it for cooking. This practice may serve to reduce the levels of potentially harmful substances like erucic acid and also diminishes the strong smell and taste of the oil. However, mustard oil is not considered suitable for human consumption in the United States, Canada, and the European Union due to its high erucic acid content, which is deemed toxic. Despite this, mustard oil with reduced erucic acid content is available. In Western countries, to circumvent these restrictions, mustard oil is often sold with labels indicating for external use only, particularly in stores catering to Indian immigrants. In North India, mustard oil is also used for massages and rub-downs, as per Ayurvedic practices, where it is believed to enhance blood circulation, promote muscular development, and improve skin texture. Additionally, the oil exhibits antibacterial properties. In India, restrictions on mustard oil are sometimes viewed as an effort by foreign multinational corporations to replace it with canola oil, a variety of rapeseed oil with low erucic acid content, often derived from genetically modified canola. Many East and North Indians, who have used mustard oil for generations, dispute claims of erucic acid toxicity, instead emphasizing its health benefits. These include its low saturated fat content, an ideal omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acid ratio (15g of omega-3 fats per 100g serving), antioxidant and vitamin E content, and the fact that it is cold-pressed (extracted at 45–50 degrees Celsius). In northern Italy, mustard oil is also used in the preparation of a fruit condiment called mostarda. Mustard Oil from Mixing Seeds with Water The pungency of mustard as a condiment arises when ground mustard seeds are mixed with water, vinegar, or other liquids (or even when chewed). This reaction occurs due to the interaction between the enzyme myrosinase and a glucosinolate compound called sinigrin, found in the seeds of black mustard (Brassica nigra) or brown Indian mustard (Brassica juncea). This chemical reaction produces allyl isothiocyanate, a compound responsible for the sharp taste of mustard. Through distillation, a highly pungent essential oil, sometimes referred to as volatile mustard oil, can be produced. This oil contains over 92% allyl isothiocyanate. The pungency of allyl isothiocyanate is attributed to its activation of the TRPA1 ion channel in sensory neurons. White mustard (Brassica hirta), on the other hand, does not produce allyl isothiocyanate but instead yields a milder isothiocyanate. Allyl isothiocyanate serves as a natural defense mechanism for the mustard plant against herbivores. Since this compound is harmful to the plant itself, it is stored in a harmless glucosinolate form, separate from the myrosinase enzyme. When a herbivore chews the plant, the toxic allyl isothiocyanate is produced as a deterrent. This compound is also responsible for the pungent taste of horseradish and wasabi. Allyl isothiocyanate can be synthesized artificially and is sometimes referred to as synthetic mustard oil. Due to its content of allyl isothiocyanate, this type of mustard oil is toxic and can irritate the skin and mucous membranes. In very small amounts, it is used by the food industry for flavoring. It is also employed as a repellent for cats and dogs and can denature alcohol, rendering it unfit for human consumption and thereby avoiding taxes on alcoholic beverages. The CAS number for this type of mustard oil is 8007-40-7, while the CAS number for pure allyl isothiocyanate is 57-06-7. Cultural and Traditional Uses In Punjabi weddings, mustard oil is traditionally used as fuel for the ceremonial jaggo pot. It is also incorporated into homemade cosmetics during the pre-wedding ritual of mayian. Additionally, mustard oil is often used to welcome a newlywed couple, a son or daughter returning after a long absence, or someone who has succeeded in exams or elections.
